31251-the-book-of-pears-and-plums-with-c:
The Reverend E. Bartrum's Book of Pears and Plums was published by John Lane at the Bodley Head in 1903 as number eleven in the Handbooks of Practical Gardening, edited by Harry Roberts. It is a thorough fruit-grower's manual. Pear chapters cover history, situation and soil, protection, planting, staking and wiring, stocks, and the training of orchard, pyramid, columnar, espalier, fan, bush, cordon, and arch trees.

Further chapters treat manures, pears for private gardens, exhibition, cooking, early, late, and cottagers' pears, synonyms, and pears for perry. They also cover gathering and storing, insect enemies, pruning, and marketing, with added chapters on cherries and mulberries. Practical and detailed, the book served Edwardian gardeners planting for table and show.
33044-birds-from-north-borneo-university:
Max C. Thompson's Birds from North Borneo reports on bird specimens collected in North Borneo. It was published as volume seventeen, number eight of the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, on October 27, 1966. The paper, running from page 377 to 433 with one figure, gives descriptions of specimens with notes on male and female birds, drawn from museum collections and field work. It was issued for libraries and workers in the field through the museum's exchange system.

As a faunal paper, its value lies in careful, comparable records: which birds were found where, how they looked, and how they fit the known birds of Borneo. Thompson writes for ornithologists, not for casual birdwatchers, and the paper's precision serves later research on distribution and variation. For students of Southeast Asian birds, it remains a solid, citable source from a major museum series.
doe-osti-2589478-updated-report-for-the-:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-5500-93534 updates a study of a gas-served smart neighborhood, prepared for Nicor Gas under agreement TSA-24-24894. Authors Xin Jin, Jeff Maguire, Michael Blonsky, and Prateek Munankarmi revisit an earlier design study with fresher inputs. Homes in the design pair rooftop solar with equipment such as batteries, fuel cells, or generators.

New runs swap in weather from 2023 and 2024 in place of 2019, plus current energy prices and emission factors. Scenarios compare gas homes against all-electric homes, each with solar sized to reach carbon neutrality. Earlier outage tests, set in a five-day 2019 polar vortex blackout, were not rerun because no similar event occurred in the new weather years. Gas equipment homes had kept full service in those tests, and the update keeps that context.
doe-osti-2999111-dre-designing-for-resil:
Jamie Thorpe, Todd Coffey, Nicholas Jacobs and co-workers at Sandia National Laboratories present DRE, Designing for Resilience through Emulation, in report SAND2025-12402, printed September 2025. Defenders cannot test cyber attacks on real control systems, so Sandia emulates them, building working copies in software. DRE wraps that emulation with statistics, so design choices can be judged with their uncertainty attached rather than by single runs.

The pipeline adds uncertainty quantification, surrogate models that stand in for slow simulations, and early optimisation work to Sandia's Emulytics tool set. A demonstration exercise runs a full case through the method. Follow-on studies chased noise in attack timing inside the CALDERA attack tool, finding most variation arose before the attacker reached the target machine. The report gathers fiscal 2023 to 2025 research, tool upgrades, a practical application chapter, and the road ahead for the pipeline.
doe-osti-3004706-development-of-an-fgpa-:
A. Singh and colleagues at Brookhaven describe a test instrument in technical note BNL-229149-2025-TECH, dated November 2025. The note supports the Electron-Ion Collider now under construction. Accelerator cavities need precise radio-frequency control of amplitude and phase, handled by a low-level RF system. Testing those controls against a real cavity, especially with beam, is rarely possible on demand.

The team built a cavity simulator on an FPGA chip instead. Digital simulation in software is too slow and awkward to wire to control hardware, while the FPGA version answers in real time and can be reprogrammed as cavity designs change. The note derives the cavity equations the simulator implements, including beam current effects. Control engineers gain a bench partner that behaves like a cavity whenever they need one.
doe-osti-3010867-artificial-intelligence:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Ying Zhang, Rachel Hoesly, Milan Jain, and Meredydd Evans, dated September 2025, applies artificial intelligence to multiscale buildings energy analysis. The setting is GCAM-USA, the state-level version of a global energy model that needs building demand detail it cannot survey directly.

A Bayesian multivariate regression ties household energy use to demographics, housing, and income for four fuels at once: natural gas, fuel oil, propane, and electricity. Estimates then aggregate to census-scale regions. Satellite imagery, parcel data, and urban form features let the models infer building types where surveys are thin, transferring relationships learned in well-surveyed regions.
doe-osti-3017158-u-s-department-of-energ:
Vanessa Stevens, Dave Wesolowski, and Michael Henderson of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this February 2026 building survey, NLR/TP-5500-93931. It was done under the Energy Department's Energy to Communities program for Moore Street Seniors Inc, a senior housing organization. A building survey is the groundwork step: measure the building as it stands before recommending energy upgrades.

The survey includes multi-point air leakage testing of the building envelope. Testers used TECTITE 4.0 software, a digital pressure and flow gauge, and a calibrated fan to take pressure and airflow readings. Interior hallway conditions formed part of the test setup. Leakage numbers matter because uncontrolled air flow drives heating and cooling costs, and comfort problems, in older housing. The report gives the housing provider a measured starting point for weatherization and retrofit decisions that affect residents' bills.
doe-osti-3625678-testing-and-validation-: Heliostats got wireless-validated, and this DOE final covers communication architecture fields. The pages detail the testing findings. The energy folks get their closeout. The SIPS was report. The closeout was energy. The fields were heliostat. The architecture were communication.
nasa-tm-19720017533-postflight-analysis-:
The Telemetry and Communications Systems Division at the Manned Spacecraft Center wrote this analysis in January 1972. It forms supplement six to the Apollo 15 mission report, MSC-05161. The subject is the radio link between moonwalkers and the lunar module. That link, called EVCS, carried the astronauts' voices and data. Apollo 15 flew the first lunar rover and longer surface stays. Clear communications were vital to its safety.

Engineers compared the link's real flight performance with preflight predictions. Apollo 15 flight data supplied the evidence for that check. One conclusion concerned the radio transmission loss figures. Those data agreed well with what planners had expected. James A McDivitt, manager of the Apollo spacecraft program, approved the supplement. Postflight checks like this hardened later mission planning.
podcast-joerogan-rUuFMjhRkmU:
Welsh writer Jon Ronson sits down with Joe Rogan in episode 668 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Ronson wrote The Men Who Stare at Goats and The Psychopath Test, books that mix humor with uneasy truths. His gentle style hides a sharp eye for strange people.

Ronson talks about psychopaths, public shaming, and the odd worlds his reporting takes him into. He shares how he gains the trust of extremists, gurus, and spies alike. Rogan asks about the human cost of online pile-ons, a topic Ronson later wrote a book on. The result is odd, humane, and very British in tone.
